## American salaries

In Lab 8, we used the **American Community Survey (ACS)** to compare average income across groups.

Today we ask a different kind of question:

> **Among employed adults, how is annual income related to the number of hours worked each week?**

Both variables are numerical, so we can move from a scatterplot and correlation to a **simple linear regression model**.

The goal is not only to fit a line. We want to understand:

- what the line summarizes;
- how the slope should be interpreted;
- how predictions and residuals work;
- how to evaluate whether a linear model is a reasonable summary.

---

## The data

Load the packages and the ACS data:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

load(url(
  "https://github.com/GarciaRios/govt_3990/raw/gh-pages/Labs/lab6/acs.RData"
))
```

Keep employed respondents with positive reported income and observed work hours:

```{r}
acs_emp <- acs |>
  filter(
    employment == "employed",
    income > 0,
    !is.na(hrs_work)
  )
```

The main variables are:

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `income` | Annual wage and salary income |
| `hrs_work` | Usual weekly hours worked |
| `age` | Age |
| `time_to_work` | Travel time to work |

Take a quick look:

```{r}
glimpse(acs_emp)
```

---

# 1. Scatterplot and correlation

Start by visualizing weekly hours worked and annual income.

```{r}
ggplot(
  acs_emp,
  aes(x = hrs_work, y = income)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours worked per week",
    y = "Annual income ($)",
    title = "Annual income and weekly hours worked"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Exercise 1

Describe the relationship between `hrs_work` and `income`.

Comment on:

- form;
- direction;
- strength;
- unusual observations.

Does the relationship look linear enough that a straight line could be a useful summary?

If the relationship looks reasonably linear, we can summarize its direction and strength with the correlation coefficient.

```{r}
acs_emp |>
  summarise(
    r = cor(hrs_work, income)
  )
```

How does the value of \(r\) compare with what you saw in the scatterplot?

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Correlation summarizes **linear association**. A scatterplot should come first because very different relationships can produce similar correlations.
:::

---

# 2. Residuals and the least-squares line

A regression line predicts a value of \(y\) for each value of \(x\).

For each observation, the difference between the observed and predicted value is the **residual**:

\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i.
\]

To see what least squares is doing, we will use the same interactive function used in the earlier version of this lab.

Load it:

```{r}
source(url(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GarciaRios/govt_3990/gh-pages/Labs/lab7/plot_ss.R"
))
```

Because the ACS sample is much larger than the baseball example for which this function was originally designed, create a smaller demonstration sample:

```{r}
set.seed(311)

acs_demo <- acs_emp |>
  slice_sample(n = 50)
```

Run the following command in the **Console** rather than while rendering the Quarto document:

```{r}
#| eval: false
plot_ss(
  x = hrs_work,
  y = income,
  data = acs_demo
)
```

Click two points to draw a line. The vertical segments are residuals.

To see the squared residuals:

```{r}
#| eval: false
plot_ss(
  x = hrs_work,
  y = income,
  data = acs_demo,
  showSquares = TRUE
)
```

### Exercise 2

Looking at the points and residuals, what does a **positive residual** mean? What does a **negative residual** mean?

### Exercise 3

Run `plot_ss()` several times and try to make the **sum of squared residuals** as small as possible.

- What is the smallest sum of squares you obtain?
- Compare with someone sitting near you.
- Why do your lines differ?

The least-squares regression line is the line that minimizes

\[
\sum e_i^2.
\]

Instead of finding it by trial and error, R can calculate it directly.

---

# 3. The linear model

Fit a simple linear regression model using weekly hours to predict annual income:

```{r}
income_hours_model <- lm(
  income ~ hrs_work,
  data = acs_emp
)

summary(income_hours_model)
```

The formula

```
income ~ hrs_work
```

means:

> Model **annual income** as a function of **weekly hours worked**.

The fitted regression equation has the form

\[
\widehat{income}
=
b_0+b_1(hrs\_work).
\]

The coefficient table gives us estimates of \(b_0\) and \(b_1\).

### Exercise 4

Using the model output:

1. Write the fitted regression equation.
2. Interpret the slope in context.
3. Interpret the intercept mathematically.
4. Is the intercept substantively meaningful here?

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
The slope describes an **association** in these observational data. It does not mean that increasing someone's weekly hours would necessarily cause income to rise by exactly the slope.
:::

---

## Add the regression line

Plot the least-squares line on top of the data:

```{r}
ggplot(
  acs_emp,
  aes(x = hrs_work, y = income)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Hours worked per week",
    y = "Annual income ($)",
    title = "Annual income and weekly hours worked",
    subtitle = "Least-squares regression line"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The model summary also reports **Multiple R-squared**, or simply \(R^2\).

\(R^2\) is the proportion of variability in the response variable accounted for by the fitted linear model.

### Exercise 5

1. Report \(R^2\).
2. Interpret it in context.
3. Compare \(R^2\) with the correlation you calculated earlier. Remember that in simple linear regression,

\[
R^2=r^2.
\]

---

# 4. Compare another predictor

The earlier version of this lab compared several possible predictors of the same outcome. We will do the same with ACS data.

Fit a model using `age` to predict annual income:

```{r}
income_age_model <- lm(
  income ~ age,
  data = acs_emp
)

summary(income_age_model)
```

### Exercise 6

For the age model:

1. Write the regression equation.
2. Interpret the slope.
3. Report \(R^2\).
4. Which variable accounts for more variation in annual income: `hrs_work` or `age`?

Before deciding which model is more useful, also inspect the scatterplot:

```{r}
ggplot(
  acs_emp,
  aes(x = age, y = income)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Does a straight line describe the age-income relationship equally well across the full age range?

---

# 5. Prediction and prediction errors

Use the hours-worked model to predict annual income for someone who reports working 40 hours per week:

```{r}
predict(
  income_hours_model,
  newdata = data.frame(
    hrs_work = 40
  )
)
```

Now choose one observed respondent who reports 40 hours:

```{r}
example_worker <- acs_emp |>
  filter(hrs_work == 40) |>
  slice(1)

example_worker |>
  select(hrs_work, income)
```

Calculate the predicted value and residual:

```{r}
example_prediction <- predict(
  income_hours_model,
  newdata = example_worker
)

example_worker |>
  transmute(
    hrs_work,
    income,
    predicted_income = as.numeric(example_prediction),
    residual = income - as.numeric(example_prediction)
  )
```

### Exercise 7

For this respondent:

1. What income does the model predict?
2. What income was observed?
3. What is the residual?
4. Did the model overpredict or underpredict income?

---

## Extrapolation

Check the observed range of weekly work hours:

```{r}
range(acs_emp$hrs_work)
```

Predictions within the observed range are generally more defensible than predictions far outside it.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
R will calculate a prediction for almost any value you give it. That does not mean the linear relationship should be assumed to continue beyond the observed data.
:::

---

# 6. Model diagnostics

The earlier lab checked whether the fitted line was a reasonable model by examining the residuals. We will do the same here.

Create a small data frame containing fitted values and residuals:

```{r}
model_check <- tibble(
  fitted = fitted(income_hours_model),
  residual = resid(income_hours_model)
)
```

## Linearity and constant variability

```{r}
ggplot(
  model_check,
  aes(x = fitted, y = residual)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.30) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Fitted income",
    y = "Residual",
    title = "Residuals versus fitted values"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Exercise 8

Is there an obvious pattern in the residuals?

Does the spread of the residuals remain roughly constant across fitted values?

What does this tell you about the limitations of using a simple linear model for income?

---

## Nearly normal residuals

```{r}
ggplot(
  model_check,
  aes(x = residual)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 20
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Residual",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Distribution of regression residuals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Exercise 9

Do the residuals appear approximately normal?

What features of the income data might explain the shape you see?

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A model can reveal a real association and still be an imperfect description of the data. Model diagnostics help us see what the simple line is leaving out.
:::
